screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Brain Health & Psychology queue positions 11-90. Drafted by Claude Haiku 5.5 and claim-audited against source text by Claude Opus 5.5 (docs/haiku-calibration/).

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Phytochemicals for Improving Aspects of Cognitive Function and Psychological State Potentially Relevant to Sports Performance.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review with no described search method, covering human controlled-trial evidence on phenolics, terpenes, triterpenes and alkaloids for attention, memory, alertness and mood, drawn mainly from healthy non-athlete samples. The author reports consistent cardiovascular benefits of polyphenols, mixed cognitive results for most compounds, and almost no evidence from sporting contexts.
records.limitations: Because no search method is described, study selection cannot be checked, and the review does not describe a quality appraisal. The author discloses research grants and consultancy from companies with an interest in phytochemicals, and the article was part of a supplement sponsored by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the cognitive and mood findings as performance benefits for athletes, when the review itself says the sporting-context evidence is almost absent and that most findings come from healthy, mostly non-athletic samples.

changes: paper.athleteDev: 'identifies no sport-specific trial showing that phytochemicals improve performance' -> notes the single 15-athlete triterpene study ('improved reaction times ... in a small sample of 15 athletes') and the 30-participant peppermint oil study ('the only study to date involving physical performance')

records.sourceFile: Public chronic traumatic encephalopathy knowledge - Sources, accuracy and confidence.pdf
records.degradedReason: The article's own DOI is not printed in the extracted text. The only DOIs present are reference-list DOIs (10.1177/01461672221117691 and 10.1201/b18959-7). The operator may verify the DOI externally and upgrade the decision.

changes: paper.practicalImplications: example read as if 'CTE is diagnosed only after death' were the error -> the error is not knowing this (only 33.21% answered 'CTE can only be diagnosed after death' correctly as True; 33.01% knew single-event causation is False)
paper.findings: 'largest estimated sources' -> 'named sources the authors identify as most used' ('Other' averaged 12.76%, above social media 10.14%, Table 3)
DOI: confirmed no own DOI anywhere in the text (only reference-list DOIs at lines 363-379); DEGRADED with doiMissing kept
verification.residualConcerns: Own DOI not printed; operator should verify externally before upgrading. Article is labelled 'Special Communication' but reports original survey data.
